Machine Basics, DC Machines and Rotating Fields (Ch4–6)

Why this matters in the exam: Q3(a) of both past papers tests this material directly. Jun23 Q3a (6 marks) asks for poles from rated speed, synchronous or induction, ideal efficiency, and speed and power on a linear τ–n curve. Jun24 Q3a (6 marks) asks you to name and sketch the synchronous, DC and induction τ–n curves, and to say how to halve their speed safely. The 2023 quiz Q1 (5 marks) used the same power and torque basics (, efficiency, rpm to rad/s). Ch5 DC analysis (, , ) has not been a full exam part recently, but it is the model for every machine later in the course, and Workshop 5 is built on it. These are about 6 quick marks and a foundation for Q3b/c and Q4.

1.2 Synchronous speed and pole count (Lecture 4.2.1–4.2.2, 6.2.6)

The course writes this with p = pole-pairs:

  • What it is: the speed of the rotating stator field. A synchronous machine runs at exactly . An induction machine runs a little below as a motor.
  • When to use it: any time you are given a frequency and either a pole count or a rated speed.
  • Trap: mixing up p (pole-pairs) and poles. “8 pole” means p = 4, so rpm, not 375 rpm. Also, p must be a positive integer, so the pole count is always even and at least 2.
Poles p at 50 Hz at 60 Hz
2 1 3000 3600
4 2 1500 1800
6 3 1000 1200
8 4 750 900
10 5 600 720
12 6 500 600

Finding poles from a rated speed. Compute . If the result is an integer, the machine is synchronous at that speed. If it is not, the machine is an induction machine. Round down to the integer, because an induction motor’s synchronous speed is just above its rated speed. Example: 560 rpm at 50 Hz gives , so p = 5, rpm, 10 poles.

1.4 Speed control (Lecture 4.1.5, 4.1.7–4.1.8, 7.9.4)

  • DC: the no-load speed is proportional to V. The speed drop stays constant when V changes, so the curve slides sideways and keeps its slope. Lecture example: 1000/850 rpm at becomes 500/350 rpm at .
  • AC (induction and synchronous): is proportional to f. You must change V in proportion (V/f constant). The back-emf equation shows that, ignoring stator resistance, . If you cut f without cutting V, the flux rises, the core saturates and the current becomes very large. The slip speed at rated torque () stays constant.
  • Trap: for an induction machine, do not scale in proportion. 1500/1400 rpm at 50 Hz becomes 500/400 rpm at 16.67 Hz, not 500/466.7 rpm.

1.6 Rotating magnetic fields (Ch6, conceptual)

  • Stator winding: each phase is a pair of opposite coils in series. A positive current gives a field along the phase’s magnetic axis, and a negative current reverses it. The three axes are 120° apart. One phase at a time, with ±, gives six field directions. Stepping through them in order gives a stepwise rotating field (60° steps for 2 poles). A stepper motor works this way (not examinable).
  • Smoothly rotating field: balanced three-phase currents give a field of constant magnitude rotating at constant speed (PQ 6.6).
  • Phase sequence is the order in which the phases reach their peaks: abc = bca = cab gives one direction, and acb = cba = bac gives the other. Swapping any two supply leads reverses the rotation (PQ 6.5). Note that a cyclic relabelling of all three (a to b, b to c, c to a) does not reverse it.
  • Pole number: a 4-pole winding is two sets of 2-pole windings. One electrical cycle moves the field by one pole-pair, which is of a revolution. That is why .

Press Play and watch three pulsating coil MMFs add to one constant-length resultant; toggle the phase sequence to reverse it, and raise the pole pairs to see n_S = 60f/p fall.

2. The method

Type A: “How many poles? Synchronous or induction? Ideal efficiency?”

Recognise it: you are given f and a rated speed in rpm.

  1. Compute .
  2. If the result is an integer, the machine is synchronous and . If it is not an integer, the machine is induction: take .
  3. Poles = 2p, and .
  4. Ideal (maximum) efficiency of an induction motor is . The rotor copper loss is , so at best . For a DC motor the same idea gives .
  5. State the reason in one line, e.g. “560 rpm is below 600 rpm, which is the nearest synchronous speed, so the machine has slip and is an induction machine.”

Type B: speed or power at a fraction of rated torque

  1. Find the zero-torque speed ( or ) and the rated speed drop .
  2. Then . For a synchronous machine, .
  3. . Express it as a percentage if asked.

Type C: change the speed (DC voltage, AC V/f)

  1. DC: . The speed drop stays the same.
  2. AC: and . The slip speed at a given torque fraction stays the same.
  3. If you are given a target operating speed at some torque, first add back the speed drop: . Then scale.
  4. For sketches, the new curve is parallel to the old one (DC, IM), or a vertical line at the new (synchronous).

Type D: DC machine operating point

  1. Write down k (V/(rad/s)), R and V. If k is missing, get it from no-load (), from , or from . If R is missing, get it from the stall test, .
  2. Find whichever of I, E, τ, ω you are given, then chain the rest: by k, by , by k.
  3. Convert ω to rpm only at the end.
  4. Power: , , , . Check that (motor) or (generator) gives the same value.
  5. Motor or generator? Compare n with (or E with V), and check the sign of I.

Type E: rotating-field concept question

  1. Draw the three phase axes 120° apart and mark the sign of each current.
  2. Use the right-hand rule for each coil. In the course’s convention, positive gives a field pointing up along axis A, and negative gives a field pointing down.
  3. Phase sequence sets the direction of rotation. Swapping two leads reverses it.
  4. Answer in words if the question says “words only”.

4. Traps that cost marks

  • p vs poles. The course formula uses pole-pairs. “6-pole, 50 Hz” gives 1000 rpm, not 500 rpm.
  • Rounding p to the nearest integer instead of down. For an induction motor, must be above . (Rounding to the nearest happens to work for PQ 4.11, which asks for the closest to a desired speed. That is a different question.)
  • rpm in . Always use rad/s. k = 220/1500 is wrong; V/(rad/s) is right (PQ 5.3a).
  • Scaling the rated speed in proportion when you change V or f. It is the speed drop (DC) or slip speed (IM) that stays constant.
  • Changing f without changing V on an AC machine. This saturates the core and causes overcurrent. Jun24 Q3a(ii) asks for “safe” operation, and the marks are for “halve V and f”.
  • Assuming part-load power = fraction × rated power on a DC or induction machine. The speed rises, so .
  • Using . Input power is . is the converted (output) power.
  • Sign errors for generators. With I flowing out, . Generator efficiency is , not .

Jun24 Q3a (past exam, 6 marks). Torque vs. Speed Characteristics. Consider the torque versus speed curves shown in the figure below.

  1. For each curve, write the type of machine in the space below the curve and draw the resulting torque curve if the no-load/synchronous speed was reduced to half of its original value. [3 marks]
  2. Alongside each curve, indicate how you could halve the no-load/synchronous speed while ensuring safe machine operation. [3 marks]
Solution

The official answer is only “synchronous, DC, induction; sketch curves from Sections 4.1 and 7.9; halve V and f / halve V / halve V and f”. (On the paper the three plots are stacked top to bottom; above they are shown left to right in the same order.)

(i) [3 marks]

  1. Synchronous machine: a vertical line at . At half speed it is a vertical line at .
  2. DC machine: a line sloping down from at τ = 0. At half speed the new line starts at and is parallel to the original. The speed drop at any torque is unchanged, so the curve slides left.
  3. Induction machine: a steep line sloping down from , shown in its linear region near . At half speed it starts at and is parallel to the original. The slip speed at a given torque is unchanged.

The figure in Section 1.3 shows all three, with the halved versions dashed.

(ii) [3 marks]

  • Synchronous: halve the supply frequency f, which halves . Also halve V, to keep V/f and hence the peak flux constant. This avoids core saturation and large currents.
  • DC: halve the terminal voltage V. The no-load speed halves.
  • Induction: halve both f and V (constant V/f), for the same reason as the synchronous machine.

In practice the AC machines need a variable-voltage, variable-frequency inverter. The DC machine needs a variable DC supply, such as a PWM chopper like the cordless-drill example in Lecture 4.1.6.

PQ 4.3 (practice questions). A 500W DC machine has a no-load speed of 12,000 rpm and a rated speed of 10,000 rpm when operated at rated voltage.

  1. What is the rated output power of the DC machine?
  2. Calculate the rated output torque.
  3. Calculate the motor speed (in rpm) corresponding to half rated torque.
  4. Calculate the motor output power with half rated torque. Why is this higher than half rated power (250W)?
Solution

  1. The rating is the output: 500 W.

  2. rad/s, so 0.4775 Nm.

  3. The speed drops 2000 rpm at rated torque, so only 1000 rpm at half torque: 11 000 rpm.

  4. 275 W. The torque is half, but the speed is higher than rated speed, so the power is more than half of rated power.

Course answers: 500 W, 0.4775 Nm, 11 000 rpm, 275 W. All agree.

PQ 4.4 (practice questions). Consider the DC machine described in the question above except this time it is operated with half rated voltage.

  1. What is the new no-load speed?
  2. What is the new full-load speed?
  3. What is the speed corresponding to half rated output torque?
  4. Using the template provided below: (i) Draw the torque versus speed curves corresponding to operation with rated and half rated voltage. (ii) Draw circles representing the full-load torque, half-load torque and no-load operating points for the both torque versus speed curves.
Solution

  1. The no-load speed is proportional to the supply voltage: 6000 rpm.

  2. The 2000 rpm drop at full-load torque does not depend on the voltage: 4000 rpm.

  3. Half torque gives half the drop: 5000 rpm.

  4. Two parallel straight lines: rated voltage from (12 krpm, 0) through (11 krpm, half) to (10 krpm, rated); half voltage from (6 krpm, 0) through (5 krpm, half) to (4 krpm, rated).

pole-pairs. The closest integer is 5 pole-pairs, so 10 poles, giving 600 rpm. (8 poles gives 750 rpm and 12 poles gives 500 rpm, both further away.) Here you round to the nearest, because the question asks for the closest speed, not a speed above a rated speed.

  2. A synchronous machine runs at constant speed: 750 rpm.
  3. 140.1 Nm.
  4. Still 750 rpm.
  5. The speed is constant, so the power is proportional to the torque: 5.5 kW.

PQ 5.19 (practice questions). A DC machine is driven by a small wind turbine. When the wind turbine is spinning at 150 rpm the measured open-circuit voltage is 10.5 V. The DC machine has an armature resistance of 0.4 ohms. The machine is then connected to a battery which acts like a constant voltage source of 14.6 V.

  1. What is the back-emf constant of the machine?
  2. At what turbine speed in rpm does the induced voltage just equal the battery voltage? What is the machine output current under this condition?
  3. At what turbine speed in rpm, does the machine output current equals 10A?
  4. For the condition in part (c), what is the efficiency of the machine?
  5. In a practical application, a diode would be placed in series with the output of the wind generator. This diode allows power to flow from the generator into the battery but not vice-versa. Why is this diode required?
Solution

  1. 0.6684 V/(rad/s).

  2. V: rad/s = 208.6 rpm. With the current is 0 A.

  3. Generator: V, so rad/s = 265.7 rpm.

  4. For a DC generator 78.49 %.

  5. At low wind speed V, so without the diode current would flow from the battery into the machine. That discharges the battery and makes the machine run as a motor, turning the wind turbine into a fan. The diode blocks this reverse current.

PQ 6.5 (practice questions). You connect a three-phase AC induction machine to the mains supply. On turning it on you find that it rotates in the wrong direction. How do you reverse the direction of rotation of the machine?

Solution

Swap any two of the three supply leads. This reverses the phase sequence, so the rotating field (and the rotor) turns the other way. Relabelling the phases cyclically does not change the sequence.

PQ 6.7 (practice questions). Are the following a valid number of poles for an AC machine?

  1. 2 poles (b) 15 poles (c) 4.5 poles (d) 16 poles
Solution

Poles come in N–S pairs, so the number must be an even integer: (a) yes (b) no (odd) (c) no (not an integer) (d) yes.

PQ 6.9 (practice questions). Synchronous generators are designed to feed power into the power system. In order to do so, they need to operate at the same frequency as the power grid.

  1. In Australia, what is the highest speed a synchronous generator can operate at, and how many poles does this correspond to?
  2. You are designing a power-station generator for a hydro-electric plant in New South Wales. It is designed to operate at 100 rpm. How many poles should this be designed for?
Solution

  1. The grid is 50 Hz and the fewest possible poles is 2 (): 3000 rpm, two poles.

  2. pole-pairs, so 60 poles.

PQ 5.11 (practice questions, extra). A DC machine has a no-load speed of 10,000 rpm and a rated speed of 8,000 rpm when operating with its rated supply voltage of 20 V. It has a resistance of 0.5 Ω.

  1. Calculate the input current and output torque when the machine is at zero speed.
  2. Calculate the input current and output torque when the machine is at rated speed.
  3. Sketch the machine voltage-current and torque-speed characteristics on the template provided. Label the no-load, full-load and stall operating points on both graphs and indicate the corresponding induced voltage, current, torque and speed on the appropriate axes.
  4. By observation from the graphs (without doing any calculations), what is the current and speed corresponding to operation at half rated torque?
Solution

V/(rad/s).

  1. Zero speed: E = 0, so 40 A and 0.7639 Nm.

  2. At 8000 rpm V, so 8 A and 0.1528 Nm.

  3. Both characteristics are straight lines: I falls from 40 A at E = 0 (stall) to 0 at E = 20 V (no load), passing 8 A at 16 V (full load); τ falls from 0.7639 Nm at n = 0 to 0 at 10 krpm, passing 0.1528 Nm at 8 krpm.

  1. Half rated torque is half the full-load current and half the speed drop: 4 A, 9000 rpm.

PQ 5.12 (practice questions, extra). Consider the machine in the previous question. On the axes provided sketch the torque versus speed characteristics when operating at rated supply voltage and half rated supply voltage. For both curves show the values of the stall current and torque, and the no-load induced voltage and speed.

Solution

The rated-voltage lines come from PQ 5.11 (stall 40 A and 0.7639 Nm; no load 20 V and 10 krpm). At half voltage (10 V) the no-load induced voltage and speed halve (10 V, 5 krpm), and the stall current halves to 20 A, so the stall torque halves to 0.3820 Nm. The half-voltage lines are parallel to the rated ones.

  1. Still clockwise. The terminal sequence A, B, C now sees b, c, a, which is a cyclic shift of abc and so the same phase sequence. Only swapping two leads (giving acb) reverses the field and the rotor.

  2. pole-pairs, so 60 poles. At 60 Hz, p = 36, so 72 poles.

  3. 2. One electrical cycle moves the field by one pole-pair, which is half a revolution in a 4-pole machine. The field turns at rpm while the current cycles at 3000 cycles per minute.

7. Add to your open-book reference sheet

CH4-6 MACHINE BASICS / DC / ROTATING FIELDS
n_S = 60 f / p   (p = POLE-PAIRS; poles = 2p)   = 120 f / poles
  50 Hz: 2p 3000 | 4p 1500 | 6p 1000 | 8p 750 | 10p 600 | 12p 500
Poles from rated speed: p = 60f/n_R -> integer => synchronous;
  non-integer => induction, take p = floor(60f/n_R)
Ideal eff: IM eta = n_R/n_S = 1-s ; DC motor eta = E/V = n/n_NL ; DC gen eta = V/E
Linear τ-n: n = n0 - x (n0 - n_R),  x = τ/τ_R ; n0 = n_NL (DC) or n_S (IM)
  Sync: n = n_S always (vertical line)
  P/P_R = x * n/n_R   (sync: = x)
Speed control: DC -> vary V (speed DROP constant, curve slides parallel)
  AC -> vary f AND V, V/f const (slip speed constant). Target speed at torque x:
  n0_new = n_target + x*dn_R, then f = f_R*n0_new/n0, V = V_R*f/f_R
DC: E = k w, τ = k I, V = E + I R (motor, I into machine); w in rad/s = 2 pi n/60
  k [V/(rad/s) = Nm/A]: no-load k = V/w_NL ; stall R = V/I_S, k = τ_S/I_S
  Pin = VI, Pout = EI = τ w, Ploss = I^2 R
  stall: E=0, I_S=V/R, τ_S=k I_S ; max power at n_NL/2, eta = 50%
  motoring n<n_NL, E<V, I>0 ; generating n>n_NL, E>V, I<0 (E = V + |I|R)
  wind gen + battery: diode stops motoring when E < V
Rotating field: 3 phases 120 deg apart; 6 step directions; balanced 3ph -> constant
  magnitude, constant speed n_S. Swap ANY TWO leads to reverse (cyclic relabel doesn't).
